title: GPU release staging and traffic shaping catalog
author: Priya Menon
content:
Overview

This catalog documents the canonical staging lanes, traffic shaping profiles, and Terraform operator contract that the GPU fleet and CI/CD teams use for safe runtime and kernel rollouts. It is intended for infra engineers responsible for GPU releases, release engineers running snack-sized fleet rollouts, and SREs on rotation. The guidance balances:
- predictable tenant impact (SLO-driven)
- burst/spot behavior across regions
- fast rollback when regressions are seen

Why this exists

We observed two common failure modes during model runtime/kernel rollouts: (1) sudden tenant throughput collapse caused by aggressive warm-pool rotation, and (2) egress/congestion spikes when multi-region burst orchestration lands capacity in a small set of AZs. This catalog standardizes staging lanes and CI contracts so changes are exercised against realistic traffic shaping before hitting prod.

Summary of artifacts in this page

1) Staging lanes and their acceptance criteria
2) Traffic shaping profiles and mappings to GPU pools
3) Terraform operator interface (contract) and sample module snippet
4) CI job templates (Buildkite and GitHub Actions) and synthetic workload generators
5) Release checklist and rollback playbook
6) Ownership and metrics to watch

1) Staging lanes and acceptance criteria

Each change (kernel, runtime, quantization profile, or Terraform operator) must pass one of the lanes below before gradual rollout to production:

- shadow-sim: unit + synthetic shadow traffic run (local CI). Acceptance: no kernel-level OOMs, KV cache miss rate < 2% on synthetic workload, unit tests pass.
- canary-1p (single-tenant canary): 1 production tenant routed to the new variant in single AZ. Acceptance: 24h latency P95 increase < 15% relative to baseline, error rate delta < 0.1% abs.
- canary-5p (multi-tenant micro-canary): 5 production tenants distributed across two AZs. Acceptance: throughput per-tenant variance < 20% and token-cost delta within budgeted window.
- staging-scale: scaled synthetic traffic across GPU pool slice (20% of warm pool capacity) for 6h. Acceptance: SLOs hold for 6h and memory pressure stable.
- preprod-mirror: mirrored traffic at full QPS (no user-visible fallthrough) for at least 2h. Acceptance: no regression alerts, telemetry matches baseline within 95% CI.

Acceptance metrics (table)

| Metric | Threshold (pass) | Notes |
|--------|------------------|-------|
| Latency P95 | < baseline * 1.15 | Measured per-route and aggregated |
| Error rate (5xx/timeout) | delta < 0.001 (absolute) | Compare to 24h baseline |
| KV cache miss rate | < 0.05 | Synthetic workloads should exercise caching |
| OOMs / GPU | 0 | Any OOM fails the lane |
| Token-cost delta | within budgeted profile | Provided by Optimize signals |

2) Traffic shaping profiles and mappings

Traffic shaping profiles are small JSON blobs used by the release orchestrator to inject controlled gradients of traffic:

- spike-buffered: fast ramp to 30% of target, hold 30m, then ramp to 100% over 2h. Use for low-risk micro-changes.
- conservative-step: 10% increments every 30m with health-check gate. Use for kernel changes.
- regional-fanout: sequential enrich of regions to avoid AZ-local egress spikes (region-by-region roll).
- burst-suffix: preserves a 15% reserved buffer for burst tenants and preempts canary traffic if burst > 60% pool usage.

Mapping guidance

- Kernel hotpatches -> conservative-step, canary-1p then canary-5p.
- Runtime config toggles -> spike-buffered on non-critical routes, conservative-step on critical routes.
- Quantization profile flips -> staging-scale first with representative synthetic workloads.

Example profile (canonical shape)

```
{
  "name": "conservative-step",
  "steps": [
    {"pct": 0.10, "duration_m": 30, "gate": "health-check"},
    {"pct": 0.20, "duration_m": 30, "gate": "health-check"},
    {"pct": 0.40, "duration_m": 60, "gate": "health-check"},
    {"pct": 1.00, "duration_m": 120, "gate": "manual-approval"}
  ],
  "safety": {"reserved_pct": 0.15, "abort_on": ["oom", "p95_increase>0.15"]}
}
```

3) Terraform operator interface and sample module snippet

Contract summary

The Terraform operator (the fleet-release-operator) receives a release plan resource which expresses: target_variant, traffic_profile, pool_selector, precondition_checks, and rollback_policy. The contract guarantees idempotency, plan validation, and status subresource updates. All changes must be applied via the operator in CI/CD pipelines (no human-crafted TF applies to fleet pools).

Required resource fields (brief)

- name (string)
- target_variant (string) — runtime/kernel image tag or operator version
- pool_selector (map) — labels: {region, pool_type, gpu_family}
- traffic_profile (string) — one of profiles defined above
- precondition_checks (list) — list of telemetry queries that must pass
- rollback_policy (map) — abort window, auto-rollback on X failures

Sample Terraform module usage

```
module "release_plan_example" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@our-repo/infrastructure/terraform-plugins//modules/release_plan?ref=v2026"

  name           = "runtime-2026-02-10-canary"
  target_variant = "runtime:v2.14.3-kernel-3b"
  pool_selector  = { region = "us-west-2", pool_type = "warm", gpu_family = "a100" }
  traffic_profile = "conservative-step"

  precondition_checks = [
    "metric(query: 'kv_cache_miss{env:prod} > 0.05', window: '10m', op: '<'),",
    "metric(query: 'oom_count{region:us-west-2} == 0', window: '10m', op: '==')"
  ]

  rollback_policy = { abort_window_m = 30, auto_rollback_on = ["oom", "p95_increase>0.15"] }
}
```

Operator behavior notes

- Validation: operator rejects plans that target > 50% of warm pool without preprod signoff.
- Idempotency: re-applying the same release_plan should be a no-op if status.phase in [succeeded, in_progress].
- Status updates: operator writes status {phase, applied_pct, active_step, last_health_eval} to the resource.

4) CI job templates and synthetic workload generators

Buildkite pipeline sample (simplified)

```
steps:
  - label: ":docker: build release artifact"
    command: 
      - ./scripts/build-runtime.sh --tag ${BUILDKITE_COMMIT}
  - wait
  - label: ":rocket: apply release plan (shadow-sim)"
    command: |
      ./ci/apply_release_plan.sh \n        --plan-file release_plan.json \n        --lane shadow-sim \n        --dry-run=false
  - label: ":test_tube: run synthetic stress"
    command: ./ci/run_synthetic_suite.sh --profile staging-scale
  - label: ":eyes: promote to canary"
    if: "branch = main"
    command: ./ci/promote_release.sh --lane canary-1p --require-approval
```

GitHub Actions snippet for preprod-mirror validation (simplified)

```
name: preprod-mirror-validate
on: [workflow_dispatch]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Apply release plan
        run: ./ci/apply_release_plan.sh --plan-file preprod.json --lane preprod-mirror
      - name: Invoke telemetry assertions
        run: ./ci/assert_telemetry.sh --checks preprod_checks.yaml
```

Synthetic workload generator guidance

- Use the GPU traffic emulator (repo: infra/gpu-traffic-emulator) which can reproduce token distribution, KV cache prefix skew, and tail-latency patterns.
- Seed the emulator with real traffic fingerprints (anonymized) from the traffic-fingerprint catalog.
- When running staging-scale, run for a minimum of 6h with periodic forced KV-cache invalidation to exercise cache warmup behavior.

5) Release checklist and rollback playbook

Pre-release checklist (must be green)

- [ ] Release plan resource created in staging environment and validated by operator.
- [ ] Synthetic workloads executed: shadow-sim and staging-scale with no critical failures.
- [ ] Observability: dashboards updated and alert thresholds temporarily lowered for the canary window.
- [ ] Pager rota notified and release channel created (#infra-release).
- [ ] Ownership: release owner and backout owner identified.

Promotion procedure (high-level)

1) Create release_plan Terraform module in feature branch.
2) Run shadow-sim via CI and collect telemetry.
3) Promote to canary-1p with conservative-step profile and monitor 2h.
4) If canary passes, promote to canary-5p and monitor 6h.
5) Execute staging-scale for 6h. If all gates pass, promote to preprod-mirror.
6) At preprod-mirror, validate billing/telemetry and then schedule gradual production roll with regional-fanout.

Abort & rollback policy (ordered steps)

1) Abort the current step via operator (operator API: POST /release_plans/{name}/abort).
2) If immediate rollback required, set release_plan.rollback_policy.auto_rollback_on and invoke auto-rollback.
3) If auto-rollback fails or the operator is unhealthy, manually scale down target_variant on fleet allocator:

kubectl -n fleet scale deployment runtime-v2 --replicas=0 --selector=release=unsafe

4) Notify #infra-incidents and create incident with preliminary impact assessment.

6) Ownership, run metrics, and dashboards

Owners and on-call

- Release owner: infra-release-engineering (primary contact: Priya Menon)
- Kernel/runtime owners: serving-runtime team (pager: @oncall-serving-runtime)
- Fleet allocator / operator owners: eng-infra (pager: @oncall-infra)

Telemetry to watch during windows (minimum)

- API latency by route (P50/P95/P99) — alert: P95 > baseline * 1.2 for 15m
- Error rate (5xx + timeouts) — alert: > 0.5% absolute increase for 10m
- GPU memory used / GPU (OOM alerts immediate)
- KV cache miss ratio by pool — alert: > 5% abs increase vs baseline for 10m
- Warm pool utilization and reserved buffer usage — alert: reserved_pct < 0.10
- Egress bytes per AZ — alert: top-az > baseline * 2.5

Appendix: common troubleshooting scenarios

Scenario A: P95 spike in canary after a kernel rollout
1) Check operator status for last_health_eval and applied_pct.
2) Compare canary tenant tail-latency against baseline for same route fingerprints.
3) If p95 increase correlates with memory pressure, abort step and roll back kernel.
4) If p95 increase correlates with egress imbalance, trigger regional-fanout pause and rebalance traffic.

Scenario B: OOMs observed only in staging-scale
1) Halt progress and mark plan aborted.
2) Capture minidumps and GPU memory profiles from the affected nodes (run: ./scripts/collect_gpu_profiles.sh --since 30m).
3) Reproduce locally with emulator using the same prefix/key distribution.

FAQ (short)

Q: Can I manually apply Terraform to a fleet pool for emergency rollback?
A: No. All fleet-facing changes must go through the release operator. For emergencies, use the operator API which is faster and guarantees status propagation.

Q: What if synthetic workload cannot reproduce an expensive tail-case?
A: Work with the telemetry team to add a traffic fingerprint to the emulator catalog. Use a short targeted preprod mirror with the fingerprint before promoting.
